case_study_insert.main_stem: Lorne River Fabrications (LRF) is a private limited company in the fabricated steel components sector, employing a workforce of 36. Founded in 2015 by Tomas Lorne, it welds steel frames for industrial machinery makers from its estuary workshop and operates a flat structure with autocratic leadership. LRF plans to invest $540,000 in a robotic welding cell, financed by a $340,000 bank loan and $200,000 retained profit. It has fixed costs of $210,000 a year, a variable cost of $12 a unit and a selling price of $20, and currently produces 40,000 units a year. LRF faces two problems: a weld defect rate of 3.3% on frames and rising absenteeism of 8%.
case_study_insert.appendix_1_marketing_ops: Welding Quality Log — Q3 2025: The cell welded 10,000 frames last quarter at a weld defect rate of 3.3%, down from 4.9% a year earlier. Rework costs $18 per defective frame and complaints fell from 27 to 15 a month. Delivery time is 5.2 days. A survey of 300 machinery buyers found 59% would pay $0.50 more for certified welds and 44% check supplier certification. Nine of the 36 welders lack robotic-welding training; a course costs $950 per welder, and a team working pilot has started on the cell.

appendix_2_financial_data.title: Extract from the Statement of Financial Position of Lorne River Fabrications as at 31 March 2025 ($ '000)

case_study_insert.appendix_3_external_environment: Economic and Business Bulletin (November 2026): (1) The central bank has raised the base interest rate from 4.50% to 5.25%, increasing borrowing costs for firms with variable-rate loans. (2) The national minimum wage will rise by 6.4% from $13.10 to $13.94 an hour from April 2026, lifting total wage bills. (3) Steel input costs have risen 8.1% year-on-year, energy price inflation is 7.3%, and orders for industrial machinery grew 3.6% over the same period.

questions.question_text: LRF is funding its $540,000 welding cell with a $340,000 bank loan and retained profit. Explain two advantages for LRF of using the $200,000 retained profit instead of more bank borrowing.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Retained profit carries no interest or repayment, so LRF avoids adding to the $340,000 bank loan while it already has fixed costs of $210,000 a year and an 8% absence problem. The $200,000 can fund the robotic cell directly, leaving the $8 contribution on each frame to cover rework at $18 per defective frame and the 7.3% energy inflation rather than finance charges.

Point 2: Using internal funds keeps control with Tomas Lorne and avoids further collateral, so the flat, autocratic firm is not answerable to another lender as it retools the workshop. It also preserves borrowing headroom for the $18-per-frame rework problem and for the $950 welder course: if the 3.3% defect rate delays the 40,000-unit target, LRF can draw on unused credit rather than default on an enlarged loan. Since the insert gives no loan interest rate, no exact saving can be quantified; the clear advantage is that no fixed charge attaches to the $200,000.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid advantage identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual explanation applied to LRF's investment, costs and financing.

questions.question_text: LRF wants to learn why machinery buyers value certified welds. Consider a posted survey, focus groups, or observation at trade counters. Which should LRF use to research these buyers? Justify your recommendation.
questions.model_answer:
Posted survey: A questionnaire sent to the 300 machinery buyers in the insert can reach many respondents cheaply and produce figures such as the 59% who would pay $0.50 more for certified welds. It is easy to tabulate. However, response rates are often low, closed questions cannot explain why 44% check supplier certification, and the 5.2-day delivery context is hard to capture in a form.

Focus groups: Bringing together a small number of buyers lets LRF probe attitudes to certification and rework quality in depth, generating ideas for the $540,000 welding cell. The discussion is rich and can explain the reasons behind the 59% premium. The drawbacks are high organising cost and a small, unrepresentative sample, so findings cannot be treated as a reliable measure of the whole market, and a 36-employee firm has limited research staff.

Observation at trade counters: Watching buyers choose frames shows real behaviour rather than stated opinions and can reveal whether certification badges are noticed during the 5.2-day ordering process. It is cheap and natural. The weakness is that it reveals what buyers do, not why, and is slow, so it cannot explain the 44% who say they check certification or quantify demand for the $0.50 premium.

Recommendation: LRF should use a posted survey as the primary method, backed by one focus group. The survey quantifies the 59% premium and 44% certification check across a large sample at low cost, while the focus group explains the reasons behind those answers. Focus groups alone are rejected as unrepresentative and expensive, and observation is rejected because it cannot explain motivations; together the two methods make the $540,000 investment better targeted.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Limited outline of the three research methods with minimal application to LRF.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Detailed discussion of advantages and disadvantages of at least two methods in the context of LRF with some judgement.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Detailed evaluation of all three methods in the context of LRF with a justified recommendation explaining why focus groups alone and observation are rejected.

questions.question_text: LRF has a 3.3% weld defect rate and 8% absenteeism. Explain two benefits for LRF of using team working among its welders.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Team working lets welders share checks on each frame, so faults causing the 3.3% defect rate are caught before rework at $18 a frame is needed. With a workforce of 36 and nine staff lacking robotic-welding training, peers can coach one another during the $950 course, protecting the 10,000 frames welded last quarter and the $8 contribution per unit.

Point 2: Teams create social support that can reduce the 8% absenteeism, because members cover for one another and feel responsible to colleagues rather than only to Tomas Lorne's autocratic instructions. A team working pilot already started on the cell can spread practical ideas about the robotic equipment, helping the $540,000 investment reach 40,000 units while keeping the 5.2-day delivery promise. Peer checks also reduce the $18 rework cost per defective frame, and with autocratic leadership team working gives welders a limited voice without changing overall control. The nine welders without training gain confidence faster when a teammate demonstrates each weld.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid benefit identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual development linked to LRF's defects, absence and training.

questions.question_text: LRF must prepare nine welders for the robotic cell. Consider a formal induction programme or on-the-job coaching alongside experienced welders. Which should LRF choose? Justify your decision.
questions.model_answer:
Formal induction: A structured induction introduces the nine welders to safety rules, the cell's controls and LRF's quality standards before they touch the robot, which suits an autocratic manager who wants clear procedures. It can reduce early mistakes that would worsen the 3.3% defect rate. The drawbacks are time away from producing the 10,000 frames a quarter and generic content that may not cover the exact welding faults behind the $18-per-frame rework cost.

On-the-job coaching: Coaching beside experienced welders teaches the precise settings and inspection habits needed on LRF's own cell, with no course fee and no loss of supervision. It can be delivered while the team working pilot runs and can be combined with the $950 course later. Its weaknesses are that busy mentors may pass on bad habits, coaching is uneven, and with 8% absenteeism there may not always be a mentor available.

Decision: LRF should choose on-the-job coaching first, followed by a short formal induction on safety and the $950 certified course. Coaching targets the practical causes of the 3.3% defect rate and keeps output moving while the $540,000 cell beds in. A formal induction alone is rejected because generic classroom time cannot fix LRF-specific weld faults and would remove nine people from the line; it is useful only as a safety supplement. Coaching also fits the team working pilot and the 36-strong workshop, where nine people learning together can be supported by existing welders during the 5.2-day delivery cycle. The $950 course can follow once basic welding is safe.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Basic description of the two training approaches with limited application to LRF.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Detailed analysis of benefits and drawbacks of both approaches in the context of LRF.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Comprehensive evaluation of both approaches in the context of LRF with a justified decision covering cost, relevance and disruption.

questions.question_text: Calculate and explain how LRF's management can use its cost and break-even data.

sub_parts.model_answer: Formula: Break-even output = Fixed costs ÷ Contribution per unit. Substitution: $210,000 ÷ ($20 − $12) = $210,000 ÷ $8 = 26,250 units. Answer: break-even output is 26,250 units a year.
Formula: Contribution per unit = Selling price − Variable cost per unit. Substitution: $20 − $12 = $8. Answer: contribution per unit is $8.

sub_parts.question_text: Explain four ways LRF's management can use this financial data.
sub_parts.model_answer:
1. Break-even of 26,250 units against output of 40,000 units gives a margin of safety of 13,750 units, showing how far machinery orders can fall before the $540,000 welding cell stops covering costs.
2. Contribution of $8 a frame lets managers assess the 59% of surveyed buyers who would pay $0.50 more for certified welds: that premium would raise contribution to $8.50 and can be compared with the $18 rework cost of a defective frame.
3. The $340,000 bank loan can be judged against 26,250-unit break-even; beyond it each frame adds $8, so managers can check the cell services repayments before taking more debt.
4. Unit cost ($210,000 ÷ 40,000 units + $12 = $17.25 a frame) benchmarks the 10,000 frames welded last quarter and helps quantify the cost of the 3.3% defect rate and 8% absenteeism, guiding the $950 training spend.

questions.model_answer: (i) Break-even output = 26,250 units | (ii) Contribution per unit = $8 | (iii) Four contextual uses: margin of safety of 13,750 units; $0.50 certified-weld premium modelling on the $8 contribution; loan servicing on the $340,000 borrowing; and unit-cost benchmarking at $17.25 to price the 3.3% defect rate.

working_marks: 1 mark for correct formula/method and 1 mark for accurate numerical answer in (i) and (ii). 1 mark per valid applied point in (iii).

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 2, evaluate LRF's financial position by calculating the current ratio and the acid test ratio for 2024 and 2025. Has LRF's financial position improved? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Calculations:
Current Ratio 2024 = 1.36 : 1
Current Ratio 2025 = 1.64 : 1
Acid Test Ratio 2024 = 0.88 : 1
Acid Test Ratio 2025 = 1.08 : 1

Detailed workings: 2024 current assets = $60,000 inventories + $85,000 trade receivables + $25,000 cash = $170,000; 2025 current assets = $70,000 + $95,000 + $40,000 = $205,000. Dividing by current liabilities of $125,000 in both years gives 1.36 and 1.64. Excluding inventories: ($170,000 − $60,000) ÷ $125,000 = $110,000 ÷ $125,000 = 0.88 in 2024, and ($205,000 − $70,000) ÷ $125,000 = $135,000 ÷ $125,000 = 1.08 in 2025.

Evaluation: Liquidity has improved. The current ratio rose from 1.36 to 1.64 because current assets grew by $35,000 while current liabilities held at $125,000, helped by $200,000 of retained profit being used alongside the $340,000 loan. The stricter measure rose from 0.88 to 1.08, so by 2025 LRF can cover short-term debts without relying on steel-frame inventories — important while it pays interest on the loan and funds $18 rework per defective frame. A caution is that trade receivables increased from $85,000 to $95,000, so cash is tied up with machinery buyers; if the 5.2-day delivery is followed by slow payment, the ratios could weaken, and inventories at $70,000 also need monitoring.

Conclusion: LRF's financial position has improved. Both measures are higher, and the stricter test now exceeds 1, so the improvement does not depend on stock. Cash of $40,000 in 2025 is still a small buffer beside the $340,000 loan. The residual risk is rising receivables, so credit control should be tightened before more borrowing.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: States financial figures or changes without accurate ratio calculations.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Accurately calculates both ratios for 2024 and 2025 with contextual analysis of the trend.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Accurate calculations for both years with detailed evaluation of inventories, receivables and liabilities and a justified conclusion on whether liquidity improved.

questions.question_text: Explain one advantage and one disadvantage for LRF of using recycled steel in its welded frames.
questions.model_answer:
Advantage: Recycled steel can reduce exposure to the 8.1% rise in steel input costs and appeals to the 44% of machinery buyers who check supplier certification. It supports the certified welds for which 59% would pay $0.50 more, protecting the $8 contribution on each of the 10,000 frames welded last quarter and strengthening the case for the $540,000 cell.

Disadvantage: Recycled steel can vary in composition, which may make welds less predictable and raise the 3.3% defect rate and the $18 rework cost per faulty frame. If buyers doubt the material's quality, the 5.2-day delivery advantage could be lost, and a 36-employee firm with a $340,000 loan has little room for higher scrap during the changeover. The insert gives no premium for recycled steel, so a higher material cost has no shown offset; managerial time to verify suppliers would also divert attention from the 8% absence problem. A small trial batch would show whether the change is worth the disruption.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for a valid advantage and 1 mark for a valid disadvantage.
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual development linked to LRF's survey, costs and defect rate.

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 3, evaluate how the interest rate rise to 5.25%, the 6.4% minimum wage increase and the 8.1% rise in steel input costs will affect LRF. Which change will have the greatest impact? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Interest rate rise (4.50% to 5.25%): The increase is 5.25% − 4.50% = 0.75 percentage points. On the $340,000 variable-rate bank loan, extra interest = 0.75% × $340,000 = 0.0075 × $340,000 = $2,550 a year. This is small against fixed costs of $210,000 and disappears if the loan is fixed-rate; higher rates may make future borrowing dearer, but with $200,000 of retained profit already used there is no shown figure for further debt, so the direct effect is limited.

Minimum wage increase (6.4%, $13.10 to $13.94 an hour): LRF has a workforce of 36 and produces 40,000 frames, so labour productivity = 40,000 ÷ 36 = 1,111.1 frames per worker. The insert does not give hours worked or individual wages, so an annual wage bill cannot be derived honestly. The rise is compulsory and will lift unit labour cost unless productivity holds at that level and 8% absenteeism falls; otherwise the $8 contribution per frame is squeezed, but the size cannot be quantified from the data.

Steel input-cost inflation (8.1%): The insert does not decompose the $12 variable cost, so only a labelled upper bound is defensible: if the whole $12 rose by 8.1%, the increase = 8.1% × $12 = 0.081 × $12 = $0.972 a frame; at 40,000 frames a year that is 40,000 × $0.972 = $38,880. Combined with 7.3% energy inflation, this hits every frame and cannot be removed by fixing the loan rate, though the 59% who would pay $0.50 more offers a partial recovery.

Conclusion: The 8.1% rise in steel input costs will have the greatest impact. It attacks the $8 contribution on all 40,000 frames, with a computable upper-bound exposure of $38,880 a year, well above the $2,550 interest effect, while the wage effect cannot be quantified from the insert. Management should renegotiate steel supply and promote certified welds before treating the interest rise as a priority.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Identifies the external changes with limited application to LRF.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Analyses the impact of at least two changes on LRF's costs, revenue or financing with figures derived from the insert.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Detailed evaluation of all three changes in context with shown derivations and a well-justified judgement that input-cost inflation has the greatest impact.
